morphemes.history: -sjö names the lakes that fill the Swedish interior, the twin of Finnish -järvi.
-berg marks the rocky heights; one of the most productive Swedish endings.
-fors marks the rapids that powered mills — the coastal twin of Finnish -koski.
-vik dots the long Baltic and lake shores wherever a bay gave shelter.
-näs names the capes jutting into water, the twin of Finnish -niemi.
-by is the plain Old Norse word for a village/farmstead — it even hugs Finland's coast.
-stad marks the chartered towns; the built-form ending with no clean Finnish twin.
-holm names the islets of the lakes and the Stockholm archipelago.
-torp records the medieval clearance crofts spreading into the forest.
-ed marks the narrow necks of land where boats were once dragged between waters.
-hult, a grove or small wood, clusters across the Götaland forests.
-måla records the medieval cleared and measured plots of the Småland forests.
-boda names the old booths and shielings — seasonal huts that grew into farms.
-lund, a grove, names the sacred and sheltering stands of trees from Lund onward.
-bäck follows the small brooks and streams that watered the settlements.
-gård is the plain word for a farmstead, the enclosed homestead yard.
-skog names the forest itself, marking places carved out of the woods.
-kärr names the marshes and fens of the lowland ground.
-sund marks the straits and sounds between waters, from Östersund to Stocksund.
-åker names the arable fields, the worked ploughland of the settlement.
